# AGENTS.md — ChessPulse

Working agreement for any coding agent working in this repository (Cursor, OpenCode,
Claude Code, or otherwise). **Read this file at the start of every session.** It is the
contract; the blueprint is the plan.

---

## 1. Authoritative sources

| What | Where | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Product contract | `docs/PRODUCT-DISCOVERY.md` — packet v1.0 / product v0.4, approved 2026-11-19 | **APPROVED** — do not weaken |
| Engineering plan | `docs/ENGINEERING_BLUEPRINT.md` | **DRAFT** until approved on its own terms |
| This file | `AGENTS.md` | living |
| Repository of record | <https://github.com/kernelKain/chesspulse> (public) | verified public |

Precedence when instructions collide: latest explicit user instruction → approved blueprint
decisions → product packet → defaults in this file. If two of these genuinely conflict, **stop
and say so**; do not pick one silently. Product changes are the user's decision, never an
agent's inference.

`docs/` is gitignored, so the packet and blueprint exist only on this machine. That is
deliberate. Do not "helpfully" un-ignore them.

---

## 2. The product in one paragraph

ChessPulse reviews a chess.com session the way a coach would — by looking at the player, not
only the moves — putting pulse, clock, think time and blunder rate on one timeline. A blitz or
rapid player (roughly 700–2000) plays with the app sensing; afterwards they paste their PGNs;
the app aligns local engine evaluation to the physiological trace, gates on signal coverage, and
produces one timeline, one verdict line, and a between-games coach prompt. It is a local-first
Electron app. It is **not** a chess trainer, **not** an engine overlay, and **not** a medical
device.

---

## 3. Non-negotiables

- **Local-only.** No hosted page, no public URL, no accounts, no cloud sync. (Packet amendment A3.)
- **Post-game only.** No engine, evaluation, overlay or advice while a rated game is live. The
  fair-play line is this product's ethics core and must appear in the README and the article.
- **No video stored.** Numeric samples with timestamps only. Camera consent is explicit,
  revocable, and paired with a persistent sensing indicator.
- **Refuse rather than guess.** Coverage below the gate produces a refusal, not a weak report.
- **AI never computes.** No number may appear in AI output that cannot be traced to locally
  computed data. AI panels are visually separated and labelled `INFERRED`. The app is a complete
  product without an API key.
- **No medical or diagnostic claims** anywhere: UI, README, article, video, commit messages.
- **No demo mode and no fixture path** to the report. A report requires a real captured session.

---

## 4. Authority and commits

- Default **A1**: implement one named step at a time, run local checks, stop. Git, external
  setup, installs and deployment each need separate authorisation.
- Commit mode **ASK**: no commit without an explicit instruction that names the step.
- Never, on your own initiative: commit, push, merge, deploy, install system packages, create
  accounts, change billing, or run a billed API experiment.
- Never force-push, rewrite history, or discard work you did not create.
- Planning approval is **not** commit permission.
- **Branch names say what the work is** — `proofs`, `analysis-core`, `report` — never a phase or
  step number. **Commit subjects name one change in the imperative** — "Add PGN clock parsing",
  not "phase-2 step 3". Numbers in Git history are a liability: they tell a reader nothing and
  go stale the moment a plan changes.

Prompt 2 runs at A1 with commit mode ASK. Blueprint §4 records that decision.

---

## 5. Working agreement

| Rule | What it means here |
|---|---|
| One phase at a time | The phase plan lives in the blueprint. Do not invent, reorder or merge phases; if a phase is wrong, say so and propose a change. |
| Smallest coherent step | Each step is one meaningful outcome, verifiable in under a minute; otherwise split it. |
| Explain before, not after | State approach and trade-off in 3–5 lines before a significant change. No 400-line diff followed by an explanation. |
| No unexplained code | Every non-obvious file, function and dependency gets a short *what / why / what breaks if removed* note. |
| Teach-back gate | Do not send step learning notes in chat. Write what was done, why, the data flow, and the limitation into `docs/phases/phase-NN.md`. The blueprint checkpoints stay there for the user to read. They do not pause the chat. |
| No hidden magic | No scaffolding generators, no configuration the user cannot justify in an interview. If a library does heavy lifting, name the specific thing it does. |
| Ask, don't assume | One focused question beats building the wrong thing. Use reversible defaults for trivia only. |
| Honesty about state | "Untested", "works on my machine" and "I could not verify this" are acceptable. Invented success is not. |
| Verify then report | Report `PASS` / `FAIL` / `NOT_RUN` / `INCONCLUSIVE` / `STALE` tied to the revision actually tested. |
| Repair budget | Reproduce → gather evidence → test one hypothesis → smallest fix → verify. Three focused cycles, then stop and report. |
| Interface is part of the argument | Typography, spacing, contrast, focus and every boring state are held to the blueprint's design brief (§7). "Works but looks templated" is not done. |

---

## 6. Docs and git hygiene

- **All documentation lives in `docs/`.** It is gitignored in full. Assets get subfolders:
  `docs/images/`, `docs/video/`, `docs/diagrams/`, `docs/drafts/`, `docs/phases/`.
- **Never bulk-un-ignore `docs/`.** Publishing a document is one deliberate negation line that
  the user approves.
- Maintained during Prompt 2:
  - `docs/ENGINEERING_BLUEPRINT.md` — stack, contracts, phases, acceptance criteria.
  - `docs/decisions.md` — one entry per real decision: context, options, choice, consequences.
  - `docs/phases/phase-NN.md` — what was built, how it works, how to run it, what's shaky.
- Owned by Prompt 3 (amendment P2-A). Do not draft these during Prompt 2:
  - `docs/project-qa.md` — interview-style Q&A.
  - `docs/video/script.md` — demo script with timing cues.
  - `docs/drafts/devto-article.md` — the DEV.to article.
- **`README.md` is the only documentation intended for publication.** What it is, how to run it,
  screenshots of a real captured report, article link. Honest and minimal.
- Tracked root files stay limited to: `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.gitignore`, `.env.example`,
  `package.json` + lockfile, source, `LICENSE`.
- No media loose in `docs/` or the repository root.

**Stage split.** Prompt 2 writes the technical phase notes and decision entries above. Prompt 3
writes the DEV.to article, the demo script, interview Q&A, X posts, and submission material.
Prompt 2 does not start those drafts. **Never publish, post or submit.** The user submits.

---

## 7. Secrets

- `.env` and `.env.*` are ignored; `.env.example` is committed with empty values.
- The SmartSpectra API key and any AI provider key live only in the environment. Never in code,
  logs, commits, screenshots, the article or the demo video.
- Assume the repository is public at all times.
- Validate environment variables at startup and fail with a human-readable message, not a stack
  trace.
- Never ask the user to paste a secret value into chat.

---

## 8. Engineering standards

- **TypeScript strict.** No `any` without a written reason in a comment.
- **Validate every boundary:** SDK payloads, IPC messages, pasted PGNs, AI responses, env vars.
- **Distinct, human-readable failure states** for the failures that actually happen: no camera,
  face not found / poor lighting, invalid key, rate limit, network failure during gating, low
  coverage, PGN with no `EndTime`.
- **Test where wrongness is silent:** PGN and clock parsing, centipawn-loss banding, timeline
  alignment, the coverage gate, and AI grounding checks. Do not write tests that merely mirror
  the implementation.
- **Accessibility is part of done:** keyboard operation, visible focus, contrast, a non-colour
  encoding of the "elevated" band, and reduced-motion behaviour.
- **Bound anything that costs money or touches the network:** timeouts, retries, cancellation,
  and no duplicate billed calls after an ambiguous timeout.
- **Read the SDK's live docs, not memory.** For SmartSpectra: `llms.txt` is the index, and any
  page serves markdown by appending `.md`. The SDK moves; stale syntax is a self-inflicted
  failure.

---

## 9. AI layer rules

- Provider adapter with five presets: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenCode (OpenAI-compatible),
  and a custom OpenAI-compatible base URL.
- Payload is PGN plus computed summary statistics. Never video, never a raw pulse trace, never
  the key.
- The model writes narrative, inferred-state notes and captions only. Chart geometry, verdict
  numbers, band boundaries and coach thresholds are computed locally.
- AI output is untrusted text: never inject it as HTML, and never promote a number from it into
  a computed field.
- If a provider is unavailable, the app degrades honestly (AI panel disabled with a reason),
  not silently.

---

## 10. Demo and publishing

- The video must show a **real captured session** end to end: the report at the end is the same
  session shown earlier — same date, same games, same trace. No fixtures, no demo mode, no
  re-enactment presented as live. Prompt 2 captures that session and keeps the evidence.
- Stock or AI-generated visuals are acceptable **only** for non-evidentiary segments (intro,
  transitions, concept illustration), and must be disclosed. They may never stand in for a
  session, a trace, a report or a "live" moment.
- Demo-script planning and production guidance belong to Prompt 3 (`docs/video/script.md`).
  The user records the voiceover.
- **Never publish, post, or submit on the user's behalf.**
- The consent and data-handling section in the README is a Prompt 2 deliverable, not an appendix.

---

## 11. Report in this order, every turn

1. **Where we are** — phase/step, and what this achieves.
2. **Plan** — the change in a few lines, with the trade-off named.
3. **Do it.**
4. **Verify** — how, and the actual result (`PASS` / `FAIL` / `NOT_RUN`).
5. **What this means** — 2–4 sentences the user could say aloud.
6. **Docs updated** — which `docs/` files changed.
7. **Next step** — what's next, and whether it needs approval.

Do not append a step-learning-notes block. The user reads `docs/phases/` for that material. A short "what this means" stays in the report.

Tight prose, structure over paragraphs. Assume intelligence, not familiarity with this SDK.

---

That brief was supplied as a source of working conventions, not as this project's definition.

| Adopted | Not adopted, and why |

[{"role":"system","content":"Task: Detect whether the CURRENT MESSAGE expresses frustration with an AI coding assistant.

Two consecutive user messages from a chat with an AI assistant. The AI responded between them (you can't see that response).

- **[PREVIOUS MESSAGE]**: the user's earlier message
- **[CURRENT MESSAGE]**: the message to classify

## Decision rules

Answer **true** if the user is unhappy with what the AI did.

**True signals — user blames or is upset with AI:**
- AI output is wrong: "not what I asked", "your understanding is wrong"
- AI ignored instructions: "I told you X", "I explicitly asked", "why did you change Y"
- AI did unwanted things: "why are you adding X?", "I never asked for Z"
- AI caused regression: "stopped working after your changes", "broken now"
- Exasperation at AI: "why do you keep...", ALL CAPS displeasure
- Sarcasm/distrust: "be honest", "I take your word for it.."
- Dismissing AI: "nevermind", "this is silly"
- Rejecting AI choices: "remove X. why would Y?"
- Commands to stop AI: "stop triggering X", "DONT RUN X"
- Displeasure at AI result: "still wayy too verbose", "no expressions, no charisma"
- Comparing AI unfavorably: "Google works but yours doesn't"
- "still [problem]" when AI was supposed to fix it and user sounds annoyed
- Terse negative + challenge: "no. why would X?"

**False — reporting or instructing, NOT frustrated:**
- Bug reports: "not working", "broken", "CI failed", "same error", "didn't work"
- Negatives: "nope", "no", "no it did not"
- Instructions: "fix", "try again", "use X instead", "don't do that"
- Questions: "where is X?", "seems incomplete?"
- Follow-ups: "still don't see it", "same issue"
- Behavior descriptions: "when I click X nothing happens", "it does nothing"
- User's issues: "I messed up", "ah darn"
- Pasted logs/errors without emotional commentary

Respond with ONLY a JSON object:

Attach an existing agent session that wasn't captured by hooks.

This creates a checkpoint from the session's transcript and links it to the
last commit, or to the commit named by --commit. Use this when hooks failed
to fire or weren't installed when the session started, or to attach a
research session.

How the session is linked follows from two facts about the commit — does it
already have a checkpoint, and is it pushed — the same for HEAD and --commit:
  - It already has a checkpoint: the session is added to it. Git history is
    not changed.
  - It is already pushed: the commit is left unchanged and the link is
    recorded in a new checkpoint, which is pushed right away (under the manual
    checkpoint push policy it waits for 'entire checkpoint push'). The link counts
    once the commit's author attaches it, and names that exact commit: after
    a rebase or amend, attach the session to the new commit.
  - It isn't pushed: the Entire-Checkpoint trailer is added to it, which
    rewrites it and any commits after it on the current branch (their content
    is unchanged). A trailer survives a later rebase. Merges after the commit,
    or a rebase or merge in progress, are refused. If a remote can't be
    reached to confirm the commit isn't pushed, attach refuses rather than
    risk rewriting a shared commit.

attach prints what it is about to do and asks before doing it. Without a
terminal (an agent or a script) it changes nothing and exits non-zero; show
the user what it printed, and once they agree, rerun with --force.

A session can be attached to more than one commit. Each checkpoint records the
turns since the session's previous checkpoint.

Use --review to tag the attached session as an agent review. The
first user prompt in the transcript is recorded as the review prompt.
Pass --skills to declare which skills were actually run; omit to
attach a review without a declared skills list.

<ask_user>
Use the ask_user tool to ask the user clarifying questions when needed.

**IMPORTANT: Never ask questions via plain text output.** When you need input from the user, use this tool instead of asking in your response text. The tool provides a better UX and ensures the user's answer is captured properly.

This tool presents a structured form to the user. You provide a `message` describing what you need, and a `requestedSchema` defining the form fields. The schema follows JSON Schema conventions — the input_schema for this tool already describes the exact shape.

**When to use this tool:**
- You need the user to make a decision before you can proceed (e.g., choosing between implementation approaches)
- Requirements are ambiguous and you need specific, structured input to resolve them
- You want to collect several related preferences at once rather than asking one at a time
- The user should confirm or override defaults before you act on them

**Choosing field types:**
- **Enum** — when you know likely options (e.g., database engine, auth strategy, log level). The user can still provide a freeform answer. If values are identifiers (snake_case, codes), provide labels via `oneOf: [{const, title}]` so the form is readable.
- **Boolean** — for yes/no decisions (e.g., "enable caching?", "run migrations?")
- **Multi-select array** — when the user may pick any number of values from a known set (e.g., which features to include, which platforms to target). If item values are not human-readable, use `items.anyOf: [{const, title}]` instead of `items.enum`.
- **Number/integer** — for numeric-style configuration (e.g., port, timeout, retry count). The user may still enter freeform text.
- **String** — when the answer is open-ended (e.g., project name, custom path). String answers have no length, pattern, or format restrictions.

**Guidelines:**
- Keep forms focused on one topic — don't mix unrelated questions in a single form
- Provide clear `title` and `description` on each field so the user understands what they're choosing
- Set sensible `default` values when a reasonable default exists — if you recommend a specific option, make it the default
- A single-field form is perfectly fine for a simple yes/no or single choice
- Order `properties` keys in the same sequence you discuss the topics in `message` — the form renders fields in property order, so matching the description avoids forcing the user to jump around

**Example — simple single-choice question:**
```json
{
  "message": "What database should I use?",
  "requestedSchema": {
    "properties": {
      "database": {
        "type": "string",
        "title": "Database engine",
        "enum": ["PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "SQLite"],
        "default": "PostgreSQL"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**User actions:**
- The user may **accept** the form (you receive their field values)
- The user may **decline** (they chose not to answer — respect this and proceed with reasonable defaults)
- The user may **cancel** (they want to abort the current interaction)

**When to STOP and ask (do not assume):**
- Design decisions that significantly affect implementation approach
- Behavioral questions (e.g., "should this be unlimited or capped?")
- Scope ambiguity (e.g., which features to include/exclude)
- Edge cases where multiple reasonable approaches exist
</ask_user>

**Session database** (`database: "session"`, default): persists for this session and is isolated from other sessions. Use it for structured operational data such as todos, test cases, batches, and state.

**Built-in tables:**
- `todos`: id, title, description, status (pending/in_progress/done/blocked), created_at, updated_at

`todos` and `todo_deps` already exist—insert into them; never create them.

**Todo tracking with dependencies:** Use descriptive kebab-case IDs, gerund titles (for example "Creating user auth module"), and self-contained descriptions. Status meanings:
- `pending`: not started
- `in_progress`: active; set before starting
- `done`: complete
- `blocked`: cannot proceed; explain why in the description

Record every actual prerequisite in `todo_deps`; do not infer dependencies from list order. Before inserting a dependency, insert both todos referenced by its `todo_deps` row. Todos with no prerequisites should remain independent.

Example with two dependent todos, one independent todo, and a ready-todo query:

-- Todo dependency example
INSERT INTO todos (id, title, description) VALUES
  ('user-model', 'Creating user model', 'Define the User schema and relations in src/models/user.ts'),

  ('theme-toggle', 'Adding theme toggle', 'Add an independent dark-mode toggle to the settings page');

SELECT t.* FROM todos t
WHERE t.status = 'pending'
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM todo_deps td
    JOIN todos dep ON td.depends_on = dep.id
    WHERE td.todo_id = t.id AND dep.status != 'done'
);

<ask_user>
Use the ask_user tool to ask the user clarifying questions when needed.

**IMPORTANT: Never ask questions via plain text output.** When you need input from the user, use this tool instead of asking in your response text. The tool provides a better UX and ensures the user's answer is captured properly.

This tool presents a structured form to the user. You provide a `message` describing what you need, and a `requestedSchema` defining the form fields. The schema follows JSON Schema conventions — the input_schema for this tool already describes the exact shape.

**When to use this tool:**
- You need the user to make a decision before you can proceed (e.g., choosing between implementation approaches)
- Requirements are ambiguous and you need specific, structured input to resolve them
- You want to collect several related preferences at once rather than asking one at a time
- The user should confirm or override defaults before you act on them

**Choosing field types:**
- **Enum** — when you know likely options (e.g., database engine, auth strategy, log level). The user can still provide a freeform answer. If values are identifiers (snake_case, codes), provide labels via `oneOf: [{const, title}]` so the form is readable.
- **Boolean** — for yes/no decisions (e.g., "enable caching?", "run migrations?")
- **Multi-select array** — when the user may pick any number of values from a known set (e.g., which features to include, which platforms to target). If item values are not human-readable, use `items.anyOf: [{const, title}]` instead of `items.enum`.
- **Number/integer** — for numeric-style configuration (e.g., port, timeout, retry count). The user may still enter freeform text.
- **String** — when the answer is open-ended (e.g., project name, custom path). String answers have no length, pattern, or format restrictions.

**Guidelines:**
- Keep forms focused on one topic — don't mix unrelated questions in a single form
- Provide clear `title` and `description` on each field so the user understands what they're choosing
- Set sensible `default` values when a reasonable default exists — if you recommend a specific option, make it the default
- A single-field form is perfectly fine for a simple yes/no or single choice
- Order `properties` keys in the same sequence you discuss the topics in `message` — the form renders fields in property order, so matching the description avoids forcing the user to jump around

**Example — simple single-choice question:**
```json
{
  "message": "What database should I use?",
  "requestedSchema": {
    "properties": {
      "database": {
        "type": "string",
        "title": "Database engine",
        "enum": ["PostgreSQL", "MySQL", "SQLite"],
        "default": "PostgreSQL"
      }
    }
  }
}
```

**User actions:**
- The user may **accept** the form (you receive their field values)
- The user may **decline** (they chose not to answer — respect this and proceed with reasonable defaults)
- The user may **cancel** (they want to abort the current interaction)

**When to STOP and ask (do not assume):**
- Design decisions that significantly affect implementation approach
- Behavioral questions (e.g., "should this be unlimited or capped?")
- Scope ambiguity (e.g., which features to include/exclude)
- Edge cases where multiple reasonable approaches exist
</ask_user>
<sql>
**Session database** (`database: "session"`, default): persists for this session and is isolated from other sessions. Use it for structured operational data such as todos, test cases, batches, and state.

**Built-in tables:**
- `todos`: id, title, description, status (pending/in_progress/done/blocked), created_at, updated_at
- `todo_deps`: todo_id, depends_on

`todos` and `todo_deps` already exist—insert into them; never create them.

**Todo tracking with dependencies:** Use descriptive kebab-case IDs, gerund titles (for example "Creating user auth module"), and self-contained descriptions. Status meanings:
- `pending`: not started
- `in_progress`: active; set before starting
- `done`: complete
- `blocked`: cannot proceed; explain why in the description

Record every actual prerequisite in `todo_deps`; do not infer dependencies from list order. Before inserting a dependency, insert both todos referenced by its `todo_deps` row. Todos with no prerequisites should remain independent.

Example with two dependent todos, one independent todo, and a ready-todo query:
```sql
-- Todo dependency example
INSERT INTO todos (id, title, description) VALUES
  ('user-model', 'Creating user model', 'Define the User schema and relations in src/models/user.ts'),
  ('api-routes', 'Creating API routes', 'Implement routes that use the User model'),
  ('theme-toggle', 'Adding theme toggle', 'Add an independent dark-mode toggle to the settings page');
INSERT INTO todo_deps (todo_id, depends_on) VALUES ('api-routes', 'user-model');
SELECT t.* FROM todos t
WHERE t.status = 'pending'
AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM todo_deps td
    JOIN todos dep ON td.depends_on = dep.id
    WHERE td.todo_id = t.id AND dep.status != 'done'
);
```

Create other tables as needed to load/query data (including CSVs, API responses, and file listings), store structured intermediate results, or manage workflows. Example session state:
```sql
CREATE TABLE session_state (key TEXT PRIMARY KEY, value TEXT);
INSERT OR REPLACE INTO session_state (key, value) VALUES ('current_phase', 'testing');
SELECT value FROM session_state WHERE key = 'current_phase';
```
</sql>

**Delegation**
* For /security-review or explicit requests to find exploitable vulnerabilities, invoke security-review first regardless of repository size or diff and do not review directly; do not use it merely because a broader audit includes security concerns. For all other reviews, audits, and summaries whose total evidence fits a single direct read, handle them directly; never delegate such work or split it by labeled area, angle, or subsystem, regardless of rigor or separate files.
* Delegate only work needing substantial separate context; directly handle simple lookups and known-file/immediate-output work.
* Unless the user explicitly requests a matching agent, never delegate a single continuous trace, even across many files or subsystems; follow it directly with grep/view.

* Use background explore only for concrete delegated work, never "just in case".

* Prefer custom agents over built-ins.
* Trust the harness defaults for subagents. Specify a value only when the user's current request or applicable persistent custom instructions (including global instructions) explicitly require that value for the subagent. Do not reuse values from earlier requests or infer unspecified values from the parent configuration. The runtime resolves `/subagents` preferences when these fields are omitted; do not copy them merely because they appear in `<subagent_model_preferences>`.
* Give a bounded objective/stop; request execution, not advice.
* After defining a delegated explore scope, do not use parent grep/glob/view on it before or after the task call; compile the report. Verify with tests, not repeated searches; use write_agent for follow-up.

* Do not relaunch/nest agents for the same objective or have one re-check direct work. If blocked after distinct attempts, return best evidence; use another only for a narrower question/review.
* Independent agents can run in parallel; consider side effects.
* Do not delegate work you can finish in five or fewer direct tool calls. Do not relaunch agents that return no useful output; continue directly. Use background mode only while doing independent work; do not poll.

**Background Agents**
* Need a background result before proceeding? Say you're waiting and stop. After notification, read once; don't poll or duplicate its work.

**Multi-Turn Agents**
* Use write_agent only for same-task follow-ups where retained context is useful.
* For unrelated work or the next independent batch item, use a fresh task when available rather than repurposing an existing agent. Never process an independent batch with a fixed write_agent worker pool.
* Read replies with read_agent.
* Use read_agent with since_turn to get only new responses without re-reading earlier turns.


## Security review caller contract

After the security review task completes, you MUST present the findings as a summary table using this exact format. Use the emoji indicators shown below for each severity level — these MUST be used exactly as specified for consistent color coding:

- 🔴 CRITICAL
- 🟠 HIGH
- 🟡 MEDIUM
- ⚪ LOW

| # | Severity | File | Lines | Vulnerability | Confidence |
|---|----------|------|-------|---------------|------------|
| 1 | 🔴 CRITICAL | src/auth.ts | 42-45 | SQL injection in user query | 9/10 |
| 2 | 🟠 HIGH     | src/api.ts  | 12    | Missing input validation    | 8/10 |

Then, if any issues were found, use the ask_user tool (if available) to offer follow-up actions with these choices:
- "Fix highest severity issues" — If selected, list the top issues ranked by severity then confidence, and ask which to fix. Then implement the fixes.
- "Fix all issues" — Implement fixes for all reported vulnerabilities with minimal, surgical changes.
- "Commit a summary of findings" — Create a SECURITY-REVIEW.md file documenting all findings and commit it.

If the ask_user tool is not available, present the follow-up options as a numbered list and ask the user to reply with their choice.

# AGENTS.md — ChessPulse

Working agreement for any coding agent working in this repository (Cursor, OpenCode,
Claude Code, or otherwise). **Read this file at the start of every session.** It is the
contract; the blueprint is the plan.

---

## 1. Authoritative sources

| What | Where | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Product contract | `docs/PRODUCT-DISCOVERY.md` — packet v1.0 / product v0.4, approved 2026-11-19 | **APPROVED** — do not weaken |
| Engineering plan | `docs/ENGINEERING_BLUEPRINT.md` | **DRAFT** until approved on its own terms |
| This file | `AGENTS.md` | living |
| Repository of record | <https://github.com/kernelKain/chesspulse> (public) | verified public |

Precedence when instructions collide: latest explicit user instruction → approved blueprint
decisions → product packet → defaults in this file. If two of these genuinely conflict, **stop
and say so**; do not pick one silently. Product changes are the user's decision, never an
agent's inference.

`docs/` is gitignored, so the packet and blueprint exist only on this machine. That is
deliberate. Do not "helpfully" un-ignore them.

---

## 2. The product in one paragraph

ChessPulse reviews a chess.com session the way a coach would — by looking at the player, not
only the moves — putting pulse, clock, think time and blunder rate on one timeline. A blitz or
rapid player (roughly 700–2000) plays with the app sensing; afterwards they paste their PGNs;
the app aligns local engine evaluation to the physiological trace, gates on signal coverage, and
produces one timeline, one verdict line, and a between-games coach prompt. It is a local-first
Electron app. It is **not** a chess trainer, **not** an engine overlay, and **not** a medical
device.

---

## 3. Non-negotiables

- **Local-only.** No hosted page, no public URL, no accounts, no cloud sync. (Packet amendment A3.)
- **Post-game only.** No engine, evaluation, overlay or advice while a rated game is live. The
  fair-play line is this product's ethics core and must appear in the README and the article.
- **No video stored.** Numeric samples with timestamps only. Camera consent is explicit,
  revocable, and paired with a persistent sensing indicator.
- **Refuse rather than guess.** Coverage below the gate produces a refusal, not a weak report.
- **AI never computes.** No number may appear in AI output that cannot be traced to locally
  computed data. AI panels are visually separated and labelled `INFERRED`. The app is a complete
  product without an API key.
- **No medical or diagnostic claims** anywhere: UI, README, article, video, commit messages.
- **No demo mode and no fixture path** to the report. A report requires a real captured session.

---

## 4. Authority and commits

- Default **A1**: implement one named step at a time, run local checks, stop. Git, external
  setup, installs and deployment each need separate authorisation.
- Commit mode **ASK**: no commit without an explicit instruction that names the step.
- Never, on your own initiative: commit, push, merge, deploy, install system packages, create
  accounts, change billing, or run a billed API experiment.
- Never force-push, rewrite history, or discard work you did not create.
- Planning approval is **not** commit permission.
- **Branch names say what the work is** — `proofs`, `analysis-core`, `report` — never a phase or
  step number. **Commit subjects name one change in the imperative** — "Add PGN clock parsing",
  not "phase-2 step 3". Numbers in Git history are a liability: they tell a reader nothing and
  go stale the moment a plan changes.

Prompt 2 runs at A1 with commit mode ASK. Blueprint §4 records that decision.

---

## 5. Working agreement

| Rule | What it means here |
|---|---|
| One phase at a time | The phase plan lives in the blueprint. Do not invent, reorder or merge phases; if a phase is wrong, say so and propose a change. |
| Smallest coherent step | Each step is one meaningful outcome, verifiable in under a minute; otherwise split it. |
| Explain before, not after | State approach and trade-off in 3–5 lines before a significant change. No 400-line diff followed by an explanation. |
| No unexplained code | Every non-obvious file, function and dependency gets a short *what / why / what breaks if removed* note. |
| Teach-back gate | Do not send step learning notes in chat. Write what was done, why, the data flow, and the limitation into `docs/phases/phase-NN.md`. The blueprint checkpoints stay there for the user to read. They do not pause the chat. |
| No hidden magic | No scaffolding generators, no configuration the user cannot justify in an interview. If a library does heavy lifting, name the specific thing it does. |
| Ask, don't assume | One focused question beats building the wrong thing. Use reversible defaults for trivia only. |
| Honesty about state | "Untested", "works on my machine" and "I could not verify this" are acceptable. Invented success is not. |
| Verify then report | Report `PASS` / `FAIL` / `NOT_RUN` / `INCONCLUSIVE` / `STALE` tied to the revision actually tested. |
| Repair budget | Reproduce → gather evidence → test one hypothesis → smallest fix → verify. Three focused cycles, then stop and report. |
| Interface is part of the argument | Typography, spacing, contrast, focus and every boring state are held to the blueprint's design brief (§7). "Works but looks templated" is not done. |

---

## 6. Docs and git hygiene

- **All documentation lives in `docs/`.** It is gitignored in full. Assets get subfolders:
  `docs/images/`, `docs/video/`, `docs/diagrams/`, `docs/drafts/`, `docs/phases/`.
- **Never bulk-un-ignore `docs/`.** Publishing a document is one deliberate negation line that
  the user approves.
- Maintained during Prompt 2:
  - `docs/ENGINEERING_BLUEPRINT.md` — stack, contracts, phases, acceptance criteria.
  - `docs/decisions.md` — one entry per real decision: context, options, choice, consequences.
  - `docs/phases/phase-NN.md` — what was built, how it works, how to run it, what's shaky.
- Owned by Prompt 3 (amendment P2-A). Do not draft these during Prompt 2:
  - `docs/project-qa.md` — interview-style Q&A.
  - `docs/video/script.md` — demo script with timing cues.
  - `docs/drafts/devto-article.md` — the DEV.to article.
- **`README.md` is the only documentation intended for publication.** What it is, how to run it,
  screenshots of a real captured report, article link. Honest and minimal.
- Tracked root files stay limited to: `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `.gitignore`, `.env.example`,
  `package.json` + lockfile, source, `LICENSE`.
- No media loose in `docs/` or the repository root.

**Stage split.** Prompt 2 writes the technical phase notes and decision entries above. Prompt 3
writes the DEV.to article, the demo script, interview Q&A, X posts, and submission material.
Prompt 2 does not start those drafts. **Never publish, post or submit.** The user submits.

---

## 7. Secrets

- `.env` and `.env.*` are ignored; `.env.example` is committed with empty values.
- The SmartSpectra API key and any AI provider key live only in the environment. Never in code,
  logs, commits, screenshots, the article or the demo video.
- Assume the repository is public at all times.
- Validate environment variables at startup and fail with a human-readable message, not a stack
  trace.
- Never ask the user to paste a secret value into chat.

---

## 8. Engineering standards

- **TypeScript strict.** No `any` without a written reason in a comment.
- **Validate every boundary:** SDK payloads, IPC messages, pasted PGNs, AI responses, env vars.
- **Distinct, human-readable failure states** for the failures that actually happen: no camera,
  face not found / poor lighting, invalid key, rate limit, network failure during gating, low
  coverage, PGN with no `EndTime`.
- **Test where wrongness is silent:** PGN and clock parsing, centipawn-loss banding, timeline
  alignment, the coverage gate, and AI grounding checks. Do not write tests that merely mirror
  the implementation.
- **Accessibility is part of done:** keyboard operation, visible focus, contrast, a non-colour
  encoding of the "elevated" band, and reduced-motion behaviour.
- **Bound anything that costs money or touches the network:** timeouts, retries, cancellation,
  and no duplicate billed calls after an ambiguous timeout.
- **Read the SDK's live docs, not memory.** For SmartSpectra: `llms.txt` is the index, and any
  page serves markdown by appending `.md`. The SDK moves; stale syntax is a self-inflicted
  failure.

---

## 9. AI layer rules

- Provider adapter with five presets: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, OpenCode (OpenAI-compatible),
  and a custom OpenAI-compatible base URL.
- Payload is PGN plus computed summary statistics. Never video, never a raw pulse trace, never
  the key.
- The model writes narrative, inferred-state notes and captions only. Chart geometry, verdict
  numbers, band boundaries and coach thresholds are computed locally.
- AI output is untrusted text: never inject it as HTML, and never promote a number from it into
  a computed field.
- If a provider is unavailable, the app degrades honestly (AI panel disabled with a reason),
  not silently.

---

## 10. Demo and publishing

- The video must show a **real captured session** end to end: the report at the end is the same
  session shown earlier — same date, same games, same trace. No fixtures, no demo mode, no
  re-enactment presented as live. Prompt 2 captures that session and keeps the evidence.
- Stock or AI-generated visuals are acceptable **only** for non-evidentiary segments (intro,
  transitions, concept illustration), and must be disclosed. They may never stand in for a
  session, a trace, a report or a "live" moment.
- Demo-script planning and production guidance belong to Prompt 3 (`docs/video/script.md`).
  The user records the voiceover.
- **Never publish, post, or submit on the user's behalf.**
- The consent and data-handling section in the README is a Prompt 2 deliverable, not an appendix.

---

## 11. Report in this order, every turn

1. **Where we are** — phase/step, and what this achieves.
2. **Plan** — the change in a few lines, with the trade-off named.
3. **Do it.**
4. **Verify** — how, and the actual result (`PASS` / `FAIL` / `NOT_RUN`).
5. **What this means** — 2–4 sentences the user could say aloud.
6. **Docs updated** — which `docs/` files changed.

Tight prose, structure over paragraphs. Assume intelligence, not familiarity with this SDK.

One issue: in the start handler, `if (!currentConsent()) { await stopEverything('user')... }`. If a revocation's `stopEverything` is already in flight, we return the same promise — fine.

But: `stopEverything` is defined before `defaultDataRoot` usage... order of function declarations is fine (hoisted function declarations; `defaultDataRoot` is an import).

Another subtle issue: `stopEverything` assigns `stoppingSession = run.finally(...)`. If `run` rejects, `stoppingSession` is a rejected promise; the IPC handler `return stopEverything('user')` propagates the rejection to the renderer (correct — the renderer shows "could not be stopped"). But the `window-all-closed` / onRevoked paths use `.catch`. Since an unhandled rejection would crash Node, and `run.finally()` creates a derived promise... Note: `run.finally()` — if `run` rejects, the returned promise rejects; and there is a *second* consumer? `stoppingSession` is the finally-derived promise. `run` itself has no other handler → but `finally` registers handlers on `run`, so `run` is handled. The derived promise is returned to the caller, which handles it. OK.

But careful: in `window-all-closed`, `stopEverything(...)` returns `stoppingSession`; we `.catch()`. Fine.

Now one more important consideration for finding 1: "overlapping stop requests ... cannot close the session ... until the in-progress stop has fully completed". With `stoppingSession`, the second caller gets the same promise → waits. ✔ And "window-close followed by quit cannot ... exit the process until the in-progress stop has fully completed" → before-quit checks `stoppingSession`. ✔

Also: `stopCapture` sets `capture = null` immediately, so during teardown `capture` is null and `stoppingSession` covers the guard. The start handler checks `if (capture) throw` then awaits `stoppingSession`. ✔

## Review fixes (Session 11)

Verified each finding against the code before changing anything. All eleven were still valid; each
fix is minimal and covered by a check.

1. `src/main/index.ts` — overlapping stops: `stopCapture()` cleared `capture` and then awaited, so a
   second caller returned at once and finalized the session while the SDK was still draining, and
   `before-quit` let the process exit mid-drain. Replaced with one shared `stoppingSession`
   promise (`stopEverything`) used by the IPC handler, consent withdrawal, window close and quit;
   `before-quit` now waits for an in-flight stop, and the per-window `closed` hook became
   `window-all-closed`, which also finalizes on macOS.
2. `src/main/index.ts` — start race: consent was checked only at handler entry, so a withdrawal
   during `await startSession` still opened the camera. Consent is now re-checked immediately
   before `startCapture` with no await in between, and any in-flight stop is awaited first.
3. `src/main/index.ts` — revocation released the camera but left the session header open, so the
   next launch classified it as a crash. Revoke, window close and quit now go through
   `stopEverything`, which stops capture and then `stopSession`; the shared promise prevents a
   duplicate finalization when the page also asks to stop.
4. `src/renderer/App.tsx` — SDK errors shared the operation-error slot, so a retryable error was
   shown forever. SDK errors now live in their own state and clear on the first new sample batch
   or `OK` validation; operation errors are never cleared by sensing traffic.
5. `src/renderer/App.tsx` — the stale-start half was already guarded (`revokedDuringStart` and
   `!grantedNow` return before `setPhase('sensing')`). The `adoptSession` half was real when an
   error arrives before the page adopts the session, so the reason is now restored after the stop.
6. `src/shared/contracts.ts` — `previewFrameSchema` accepted any byte count. It now requires
   `rgba.byteLength === width * height * 4`; the fixture was resized, a mismatch rejection was
   added, and real `downscaleRgbToRgba` output is asserted to pass.
7. `src/main/capture-samples.ts` — the floor advanced with each reading, so an out-of-order payload
   dropped an earlier-but-new sample. The floor stays at `lastTUs`; readings are then stably sorted
   and de-duplicated by timestamp (first wins, as before).
8. `src/main/capture.ts` — `session.destroy()` awaits the same `_stopAsyncPromise` as `stopAsync`
   (read from `js/ffi.js`), so a wedged pipeline could hang teardown forever after the 8 s stop
   timeout. `destroy()` now has its own 2 s ceiling.
9. `src/main/capture.ts` — a retryable error set `reported`, which then suppressed the terminal
   `kError` status, leaving the camera open with no notification. Replaced with `terminalReported`:
   dedupe still holds when a non-retryable error came first, and `kError` always shuts down.
10. `src/main/capture.ts` — accepted batches were not awaited, so finalization could read the store
    before the tail landed. Writes are tracked in a set and drained (bounded at 3 s) after native
    teardown; the rejection path still shuts the session down.
11. `src/shared/preview.ts` — height was derived from width alone, so a portrait or large square
    frame exceeded the schema's 1080 limit and the preview silently stopped. One scale now respects
    both caps; tests cover 640×480 at `outWidth` 1920 and a tall portrait frame.

Verified with `npm run typecheck`, `npm test` (155/155), `npm run build`, `git diff --check`, and a
20-second boot of the built app.

- docs/ is gitignored, so docs changes won't be committed (fine — intended).

I need to decide: one commit or several? The changes span several logical areas:
1. SmartSpectra capture bridge + preview (large feature)
2. Safe console logging (EPIPE fix)
3. Review fixes (hardening)
4. Dependency addition

AGENTS.md §4: "Commit subjects name one change in the imperative". One commit per verified step. This session arguably had several steps. But they're all uncommitted together and interdependent (the review fixes modify code introduced in the same batch). Splitting artificially could produce non-building intermediate commits — bad.

a) One commit for everything: "Add SmartSpectra capture with a live camera preview" — but that misses the EPIPE fix and review hardening. Actually the EPIPE fix is part of the capture work (log.ts only exists because of it).

c) Three commits in dependency order can't work since files are interdependent.

Let me think about a clean split that keeps every commit building:
- Commit A: everything capture-related (env, capture, capture-samples, preview, contracts, preload, consent, permission, index, App, CameraPreview, bridge, styles, package.json/lock, README). That's basically all of it.

- Commit 1: log.ts + log.test.ts + package.json test script → builds? log.ts is standalone. Adding the test file requires package.json change. Yes builds.
- Commit 2: env.ts + env.test.ts + capture-samples + tests + preview + contracts + ... but capture.ts is needed by index.ts.
- Then commit 3: capture.ts + index.ts + preload + renderer.

That's feasible but makes for artificial splitting of a single step, and package.json (dep) belongs with commit 3 while its test-script entries for env/log/capture-samples belong to 2/1.

Given AGENTS.md's "one commit per verified step" and that this was one continuous step (capture) with a review pass, plus the user said "commit and push all changes" (singular intent), I'll make **one commit**. That's simplest, honest, keeps history buildable, and doesn't fabricate a narrative.

cd /home/kernel-kain/Documents/Github/chesspulse && git commit -F - <<'MSG'
Add SmartSpectra capture with a live camera preview

The main process now owns the measurement session: it loads the key from
.env, opens the camera through the SmartSpectra SDK, stores pulse samples in
the session, and publishes validation hints and SDK errors to the page.

Measured on this machine: feeding the SDK frames from the page (custom input)
produced zero metrics events at both 16:9 and square crops, while its own
camera produced a series. The preview is therefore a tap on the SDK's
videoOutput, downscaled to 320 px, so the page never opens a second stream.

Shutdown has one owner. Capture stops before the session header closes, the
stop promise is shared by the page, consent withdrawal, window close and quit,
and teardown is bounded at every stage because destroy waits on the same
in-flight stop. In-flight sample writes drain before finalization, so the tail
of a session is not lost.

Main-process logging can no longer take the process down: a closed stdout was
an uncaught EPIPE during a measurement.

Co-authored-by: Copilot <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>
